title: From where to what: building the differential
description: How the time course turns a localization into a short list of causes. The module covers the mechanism categories, the where-by-when grid, the child's own clock and functional disorder, which is diagnosed from positive signs like everything else.
why: An examination can tell you where the trouble is, but it takes the time course to turn that address into a short list of causes.
objectives: Explain why the examination localizes and the history's time course suggests the cause, and when the history also matters for localization.
Use the mechanism categories and a level-by-tempo grid to turn a localization into a short, ranked differential.
Read a child's history against development: static, progressive, regressive or episodic, and age of onset as a filter.
Make functional neurological disorder a positive diagnosis from bedside signs, and know their limits.

sections.title: Why the time course matters
sections.content:
Every module so far has been about "where", the first word in Where Before What. This module turns to "what", the cause, and to the question that links the two, which is **when**.

For working out where a lesion sits, the examination matters far more than the history. The history, meaning the way the deficits evolved over time, points to the cause (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Take a hemiparesis. If it arrived within minutes, a vascular event or a seizure is most likely. If it developed over a few days, think of infection or demyelination. If it crept up over months, think of a tumor or a degenerative process. The address is the same in all three, and only the clock separates the differentials.

**What the examination and the history each tell you**

The examination tells you which structure is failing, and the history tells you how it is failing. A cord lesion that appeared over minutes is a different disease from one that appeared over hours, weeks or years, and no examination can tell those four apart. The history does no better on its own. "Getting worse over weeks" means little until you know whether the problem is in the cerebellum or in the muscle.

**When the history also localizes**

The examination shows the sum of everything that has happened to the patient, and that sum can include lesions laid down at different times. A third-nerve palsy with a hemiparesis on the opposite side points to a single lesion in the midbrain, but only if the two began together. If the palsy dates from childhood and the hemiparesis is new, they are probably two lesions, and the one causing the hemiparesis is probably not in the midbrain (Brazis 2011, p. 4). In children the birth history, the early milestones and old family photographs do the same work. They may show that a "new" weakness has been there since infancy.

**Localize before you weigh the tempo**

If you fix on the tempo before you have localized, you may settle on "sudden, so stroke" before checking whether the findings even fit the brain. Once you have an address, the clock chooses among the causes that can actually occur there, rather than among every cause you can think of.
keyPoints: The examination localizes the lesion, and the time course in the history points to its cause (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

A deficit that arrives in minutes suggests a vascular event or seizure, one that develops over days suggests infection or demyelination, and one that builds over months suggests tumor or degeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
The history also helps localize when findings began at different times, because two signs that look like one lesion may be two lesions laid down years apart.
Localizing before applying the tempo keeps you from fitting the findings to a diagnosis chosen too early.

question.question: A 15-year-old has a left hemiparesis. On the same examination you notice mild weakness of the right side of the face, and old photographs show it has been there since infancy. How should this change your localization?
options: Place a single lesion in the right pons, because the face and the limbs are affected on opposite sides
Set the facial weakness aside, because it is old
Treat them as two lesions of different ages, with the facial weakness an old finding and the new hemiparesis localized on its own merits
Assume a functional disorder, because the signs do not fit a single lesion
question.explanation: A crossed pattern places one lesion in the brainstem only when the signs began together. Here the facial weakness predates the hemiparesis by years, so the new hemiparesis needs its own localization. One pontine lesion would send the imaging to the wrong place. Discarding the old finding loses information, and two lesions of different ages do not suggest a functional disorder.

sections.title: The mechanism list
sections.content:
Once you have an address and a clock, you need a list of the ways nervous tissue can fail. Most clinicians carry some version of it. A good list is complete enough that nothing important is forgotten, and each category on it comes with the tempo and pattern it usually shows.

- **Vascular:** sudden, maximal at onset, respecting an arterial territory.
- **Seizure and migraine:** sudden or episodic, with recovery between events.
- **Infection:** hours to days, often with fever and a sick child.
- **Inflammatory and demyelinating:** days to weeks, often after an infection, sometimes multifocal.
- **Toxic and acquired metabolic:** hours to days, usually symmetric and diffuse, often fluctuating.
- **Neoplastic:** weeks to months, steadily progressive, with a deficit that spreads as the mass grows.
- **Degenerative, genetic and inborn metabolic:** months to years, often symmetric and respecting a system.
- **Congenital and developmental:** present from early life, static.
- **Traumatic:** sudden, with a history that usually makes the cause plain.
- **Functional:** variable, with positive signs of inconsistency (see section 6).

**Discrete lesions and systems**

A second way of dividing the list asks whether a disease makes **discrete lesions** or attacks a **system** (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5). Vascular events, demyelinating plaques, infections, injuries and tumors tend to cause discrete lesions, single or multiple, whose signs meet at a point. Degenerative disorders instead take whole groups of neurons that share a function, so their signs follow a system rather than a place. A symmetric, length-dependent pattern, in which the longest nerves fail first, is the signature of a system process and almost never of a discrete lesion.

**The pediatric additions**

Adult lists often treat the congenital and genetic categories as rare. In child neurology they make up much of the daily work, from malformations and perinatal injury to inborn errors of metabolism, the muscular dystrophies and the hereditary neuropathies. The categories an adult neurologist would reach for last often sit near the middle of a child's list.
keyPoints: Keep a complete list of mechanisms, with each category attached to its usual tempo and pattern.

Diseases that make discrete lesions (vascular, demyelinating, infectious, traumatic, neoplastic) give signs that meet at a point, while system diseases give signs that respect a function (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5).
A symmetric, length-dependent pattern points to a system process rather than a discrete lesion.
In children, congenital, developmental and genetic-metabolic causes move from the margin of the list toward its center.

question.question: A 10-year-old has had slowly worsening, symmetric weakness and numbness of the feet for two years, now reaching the lower shins, with absent ankle reflexes. Which kind of mechanism does the pattern favor?
options: A discrete vascular lesion, because it involves the legs
A system process such as an inherited neuropathy, because the pattern is symmetric, length-dependent and slowly progressive
A tumor of the spinal cord, because both legs are involved
An infection, because it has lasted two years
question.explanation: A symmetric distal pattern that climbs from the toes, with lost ankle reflexes, is length-dependent, the mark of a system process. Two years of slow progression in a child points toward an inherited neuropathy. A vascular lesion would be sudden, a cord tumor would bring a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs, and infection does not smolder symmetrically for years.

sections.title: Which map does the deficit obey?
sections.content:
The **shape** of a deficit can hint at its mechanism, because each mechanism damages tissue along its own map. A clot follows the blood supply, a failing axon gives out along its length, and a bulging disc presses on a single segment.

**The maps a deficit can follow**

- **Arterial territory.** Strokes respect the blood supply, so the middle cerebral artery takes the face and arm and the anterior cerebral artery takes the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7). An arterial map with an onset over minutes points to a vascular cause.
- **Length of the axon.** In many polyneuropathies the most distal parts of the nerve fail first, and the hands are not usually involved until the legs are affected up to the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76). The cause is then nutritional, metabolic, toxic or inherited, and the whole nerve is failing from within.
- **One root segment.** Pain, sensory change, weakness and a lost reflex that all belong to one segment mark a root (Pearl 2014, pp. 75, 78).
- **One nerve territory.** A mononeuropathy follows its nerve, whether the cause is compression, trauma or systemic disease (Pearl 2014, pp. 75, 83).
- **A level on the cord.** Loss below a line on the trunk, with the bladder involved, belongs to the cord. Trauma, transverse myelitis and tumor are among the causes (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-68).
- **A system of tracts.** Some diseases choose tracts on both sides rather than a place.
- **No map.** Tumors ignore vascular boundaries, grow between pathways and produce deficits that progress (Pearl 2014, p. 10). Several lesions at once also obey no single map.

:::deeper Diseases that choose tracts
Vitamin B12 deficiency takes the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts together (Pearl 2014, pp. 73-74). Friedreich ataxia takes the spinocerebellar tracts, the corticospinal tracts and the posterior columns (Pearl 2014, p. 64). Neither respects a level or an arterial territory. The deficit follows the tracts wherever they run, which is why a child can lose the ankle jerks and still have upgoing toes, the combination one of the figure's children shows.
:::

**Using the figure**

Sort the eight children in the figure above before you read the feedback. Two of them have different diseases that obey the same map, because a map can narrow the mechanism a long way without naming the disease.

**Reading the map with the time course**

The maps refine the division into discrete lesions and systems (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5), and they work best read with the tempo. A deficit on an arterial map that arrived in minutes is treated as a stroke from the start. Pay most attention when map and clock disagree. A deficit that looks like an arterial territory but has grown over weeks suggests a mass that happens to sit within that territory.
keyPoints: Each mechanism damages tissue along its own map, so the shape of a deficit hints at its cause.
Strokes follow arteries (Pearl 2014, p. 7), and axonal polyneuropathies follow length, reaching the hands only once the legs are involved to the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76).
Roots follow a segment, single nerves their own territory, and the cord a level (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-68, 75-83).
Deficiency and degeneration follow systems of tracts, as in B12 deficiency and Friedreich ataxia (Pearl 2014, pp. 64, 73-74), while tumors follow no map (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
Read the map together with the clock, because a territorial deficit that grows over weeks suggests a mass rather than a stroke.

question.question: A 15-year-old has had numb, tingling feet for a year. The numbness now reaches just below both knees, and in the last month his fingertips have begun to tingle. Both ankle jerks are absent; the knee jerks are present; there is no sensory level on the trunk and the bladder is normal. His parents ask for an MRI of the spine to look for a tumor. Which map does the deficit obey, and what does that imply?
options: A level on the cord, so the spine MRI is the right test
One root segment on each side, so imaging of the lumbar roots is needed
No map, because both hands and feet are involved, so a mass is likely
The length of the axon, which points to a polyneuropathy from a system cause such as a toxic, nutritional or genetic one, to be pursued with nerve studies and a search for that cause
question.explanation: Symmetric loss climbing the legs, absent ankle jerks, and fingertips that tingle once the legs are involved to the knees make up the length map of a polyneuropathy (Pearl 2014, p. 76). Nerve studies and a search for the cause come next. A cord lesion gives a line on the trunk and brisk reflexes below it (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-67).

sections.title: The where-by-when grid
sections.content:
The figure above pairs a level with a tempo. Choose one of each, and it shows the mechanisms that fit that tempo, with pediatric examples for that address. Once you have committed to a where and a when, it makes sure the obvious candidates and the dangerous ones both reach your list.

**How to read it**

The cerebellum is a good place to start. **Acute** ataxia in a young child, developing over hours to a day or two, brings post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia and a toxic ingestion to the top of the list. If the ataxia develops over **weeks**, a posterior fossa tumor moves up. Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia joins it, and should send you looking for a neuroblastoma. Over **years**, inherited ataxias such as Friedreich ataxia and ataxia-telangiectasia appear. The examination of a wobbly child can be the same in all three cases, and the clock alone moves you from reassurance and observation, to imaging the posterior fossa, to genetic testing.

The spinal cord can be read in the same way. **Sudden** weakness below a level suggests trauma or an infarct. Weakness that develops **acutely**, over hours to days, suggests transverse myelitis or compression from an epidural abscess or hematoma. Compression must be excluded first, because decompression can treat it. A **chronic** course brings a syrinx, a tethered cord or hereditary spastic paraplegia, and a **static** picture present from birth suggests a myelomeningocele.

**Limits of the grid**

The examples for each level and tempo are only illustrations. A rare disease may fit the pairing without being named, and a child can have a common disease that presents at an uncommon tempo. Rank the short list both by how likely each diagnosis is **and** by the cost of missing it. A treatable emergency such as cord compression or herpes encephalitis is acted on even before it is the most probable answer.

The grid can also be read in reverse, starting from the disease. If a disease you suspect belongs with a level or a tempo that does not fit your patient, doubt the diagnosis, the localization or the history of the time course, and re-examine.
keyPoints: A level-by-tempo grid turns one localization into several different differentials, separated only by time.
The same cerebellar examination suggests post-infectious ataxia or an ingestion over a day, a tumor or opsoclonus-myoclonus over weeks, and an inherited ataxia over years.
Rank the short list by likelihood and by the cost of missing a treatable emergency.
A suspected disease that does not match your where or your when is a reason to doubt the diagnosis, the localization or the timeline.

question.question: A 4-year-old has become progressively unsteady over five weeks, with morning vomiting. The examination shows truncal ataxia and nothing else. Using where and when, what is the most important next step?
options: Reassure the family that post-infectious ataxia resolves on its own
Send a toxicology screen and wait
Arrange urgent brain imaging, because a cerebellar process evolving over weeks with morning vomiting places a posterior fossa tumor at the top of the list
Order nerve conduction studies to look for a neuropathy
question.explanation: Truncal ataxia places the problem in the midline cerebellum. Five weeks of worsening with morning vomiting is a subacute course with signs of raised pressure, which puts a posterior fossa tumor first, so image urgently. Post-infectious ataxia is acute and improves over the following weeks. A toxicology screen suits an acute ataxia, and nerve studies cannot explain isolated truncal ataxia with vomiting.

sections.title: Tempo in a growing child
sections.content:
An adult's history is usually read against two questions, how fast the problem came on and whether it is getting worse. In a child, development adds a third, and it changes the meaning of the other two.

**Static, progressive, regressive and episodic**

- **Static.** The problem has been present from early life and is not worsening. Cerebral palsy is the model. It is defined as a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain ([Rosenbaum 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17370477/)).
- **Progressive.** The deficit itself is getting worse.
- **Regressive.** Skills that were present are lost. Regression is never cerebral palsy. It moves the differential toward neurodegenerative and genetic-metabolic disease, epileptic encephalopathy and acquired encephalitis. In a toddler who loses words, autism-associated language regression is common and belongs on the list, but the rarer, treatable causes still need to be considered.
- **Episodic.** Attacks come and go with recovery between them. Think of seizures, migraine, channelopathies, syncope and intermittent metabolic decompensation.

**Episodes without a lesion**

Some of the commonest episodes of childhood have no lesion behind them. Breath-holding spells occur between 6 months and 6 years, follow a fit of crying or a fright, and are outgrown. Night terrors begin between 2 and 10 years and are a partial arousal from deep sleep (Pearl 2014, p. 104). The where-by-when figure lists both, with syncope, as mimics. When the story is typical, there is no lesion to look for.

**Static lesions that seem to progress**

A fixed lesion can still unfold as the brain matures. A child with spastic cerebral palsy may present as a floppy infant before the spasticity develops (DeMyer, p. 273). A perinatal stroke may be invisible at birth and show itself months later as early hand preference. Preferring one hand before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/home_exam.html)). In both cases the parents are seeing something new, even though the lesion is old. The useful question is whether the child is losing skills or failing to gain them.

**Age at onset**

Age at onset is a strong filter. A floppy newborn, a toddler who stops walking and an adolescent with a new tremor draw from different groups of diseases, even when the address is the same. The where-by-when grid becomes a three-way table of level, tempo and age at onset.
keyPoints: In children, tempo includes development, so a history may be static, progressive, regressive or episodic.
Cerebral palsy is attributed to a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain, so loss of acquired skills is never cerebral palsy (Rosenbaum 2007).
A static lesion can look new as development unfolds, as when a floppy infant later becomes spastic or a hemiparesis is revealed by hand preference before 12 months (DeMyer, p. 273; Utah).
Ask whether the child is losing ground or failing to gain it, and use the age of onset as a strong filter on the list.

question.question: A 3-year-old with a diagnosis of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, who walked with a walker at 2, can no longer stand with support and has stopped using two-word phrases. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Reconsider the diagnosis, because loss of acquired motor and language skills is regression, which cerebral palsy by definition does not cause
Increase physiotherapy, because cerebral palsy often worsens with growth
Reassure the family that language often plateaus in cerebral palsy
Wait six months and reassess, because a static lesion can look progressive
question.explanation: Cerebral palsy comes from a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. Its signs can unfold as the child matures, but it does not take away skills already gained, and this child has lost both standing and speech. That is regression, so reconsider the diagnosis. More physiotherapy, reassurance and waiting all mistake losing ground for failing to gain it, and some causes of regression are treatable.

sections.title: Functional neurological disorder: a positive diagnosis
sections.content:
One more category belongs on the list, and it is the one most often reached by default. Functional neurological disorder is a problem with how the nervous system works rather than with its structure. The old habit was to diagnose it only after every test had come back normal. That habit delays the diagnosis and gets the logic backwards. Functional disorder is diagnosed the way everything else in this curriculum is diagnosed, from **positive findings** at the bedside.

**How good the signs are**

Fourteen bedside signs have controlled data behind them, 7 motor, 5 sensory and 2 gait. Their specificity was consistently high, from 92 to 100%. Their sensitivity varied widely, from 8 to 100%, and was often low, and the evidence was only class III ([Daum 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23467417/)). A positive sign is therefore strong evidence. An absent sign is weak evidence, and failing to find one does not rule functional disorder out.

Each sign shows either that a function said to be lost returns when the patient's attention is elsewhere, or that a deficit does not follow the anatomy.

- **Hoover sign and the abductor sign.** Hip extension or abduction that is weak on command returns automatically when the other leg is tested.
- **Give-way weakness and co-contraction.** Full power appears for a moment and then collapses, or agonist and antagonist pull at once.
- **Sensory signs that ignore anatomy.** Loss may split exactly at the midline, or vibration may be felt differently on the two sides of the forehead or sternum, although bone carries vibration across the midline. A field of vision may stay the same width at every distance (tunnel rather than funnel).
- **Gait.** Wild sways rarely end in a fall, the knees buckle without collapsing, and the walking improves with distraction.

:::deeper How the abductor sign was tested
In the study that introduced it, the abductor sign correctly classified all 33 patients tested, 16 with functional and 17 with structural weakness. The Hoover sign was non-diagnostic in some of the same patients ([Sonoo 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14707320/)).
:::

**When structural disease is also present**

Positive signs do not exclude structural disease, because patients, children among them, can have both. The old argument between parsimony and multiple diagnoses applies here as it does everywhere else ([Hilliard 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14762188/)). When the signs are present, make the diagnosis, explain it as real and treatable, and keep examining.
keyPoints: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis made from bedside signs rather than a diagnosis of exclusion.
Validated positive signs have high specificity (92-100%) but variable, often low sensitivity (8-100%), so a present sign is strong evidence and an absent sign is weak (Daum 2014).
Hoover and abductor signs show automatic power returning when attention is elsewhere, and the abductor sign correctly classified all 33 patients tested (Sonoo 2004).
Functional and structural disease can coexist, so making the diagnosis does not end the examination (Hilliard 2004).

question.question: A 14-year-old has a weak left leg. Hip extension on that side is absent on command but returns strongly when she flexes the right hip against resistance, and the left leg moves into abduction when she abducts the right. Reflexes and plantar responses are normal. Her MRI is booked for next week. What should you do now?
options: Wait for the MRI before discussing any diagnosis, because functional disorder can only be diagnosed when tests are normal
Make a positive diagnosis of functional weakness from these signs, explain it as real and treatable, and keep the planned investigations proportionate
Tell the family the weakness is not real, because power returns
Order nerve conduction studies, because the weakness may be peripheral
question.explanation: Positive Hoover and abductor signs are specific bedside evidence of functional weakness, and normal reflexes and plantar responses point away from a structural lesion. Make the diagnosis now and explain it as a genuine, treatable disorder. Waiting for normal tests treats it as a diagnosis of exclusion. Calling the weakness unreal is wrong and damaging, and nothing here suggests a peripheral nerve problem.

sections.title: Reading results with a prior
sections.content:
[[m01-where-before-what|Module 1]] showed that a test result is worth what the prior makes it worth, and that a single false-positive rate can swamp a vague question while barely affecting a sharp one. This section turns that into something you can do with a pen before you sign the request.

**Choosing the test**

Localization and tempo do two jobs. They choose the test, so a cord level asks for spine imaging, a length-dependent neuropathy for nerve studies and an episodic story for a recording of an event. They also set the prior, because a test aimed where the examination pointed starts with a good chance of finding the cause. Choose the one or two tests that best confirm or refute the tentative diagnosis, rather than every test that covers every possibility (DeMyer, p. 539). Unfocused "gunshot" neuroimaging produces false positives, and only careful localization avoids them (Brazis 2011, p. 1).

**Background rates in healthy children**

- **MRI.** Among more than 11 000 children aged 9 to 10 with research scans, 21.1% had an incidental finding, most needing no referral ([Li 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33749724/)).
- **EEG.** Among 382 healthy children aged 6 to 13, 6.5% had epileptiform discharges ([Borusiak 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20002145/)).
- **Genes.** Variants are reported on a five-tier scale whose middle tier is uncertain significance ([Richards 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25741868/)). A variant of uncertain significance in a gene that fits the localization and the clock is a lead worth following. One in a gene that fits neither is a distraction.

Each of these findings is common enough in well children that it needs a prior before it means anything.

**Predict the result before ordering**

Before ordering, write two lines in the notes. One gives the result you expect, and the other says what you will do with each answer. If neither a normal nor an abnormal result would change what you do, the test is not ready to be ordered. If you cannot say what an abnormal result would mean for this child, the localization is not finished.

**Results that contradict the examination**

A result that contradicts a confident localization deserves scrutiny before you accept it. Ask whether it is one of the background findings above, whether the test looked in the right place, and whether the examination needs repeating. The [[m12-cases|cases]] let you practice the whole sequence of where, when and what, with the test coming only at the end.
keyPoints: Localization and tempo choose the test and set its prior, so choose the one or two tests that best confirm or refute the working diagnosis (DeMyer, p. 539).
Unlocalized "gunshot" imaging breeds false positives (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Background rates in well children include incidental MRI findings in 21.1% at 9 to 10 years (Li 2021) and epileptiform discharges in 6.5% at 6 to 13 years (Borusiak 2010).
A variant of uncertain significance is weighed against the localization and the clock rather than read as a diagnosis (Richards 2015).
Before ordering, write down the result you expect and what you will do with each answer.

question.question: A 9-year-old fainted while standing through a long assembly on a hot day: she went pale, slumped, and was herself again within a minute, with no confusion afterwards. Her examination is normal. An EEG ordered elsewhere reports a few focal epileptiform discharges. Her parents ask whether she has epilepsy. What is the best response?
options: Go back to the story, which describes a faint and set a low prior for epilepsy, and explain that discharges of this kind turn up in some healthy children, so the EEG does not by itself make the event a seizure
Start an antiseizure medicine, because the EEG shows epileptiform discharges
Order an MRI to find the source of the focal discharges before discussing the diagnosis
Repeat the EEG until a normal recording settles the question
question.explanation: The story describes a faint, a common mimic of seizures (Pearl 2014, p. 104), so the prior for epilepsy was low. Epileptiform discharges turn up in 6.5% of healthy children aged 6 to 13 (Borusiak 2010). Medication would treat the tracing, an MRI would chase an unpredicted finding, and repeating the EEG until it is normal is shopping for an answer.

quiz.question: Two children have identical examinations: weak legs, a sensory level at the umbilicus and urinary retention. One developed it over 20 minutes during a trampoline accident, the other over two days after a cold. What does the difference tell you?
options: Nothing, because the localization is the same
That one of them must have a functional disorder
That the cause differs: trauma or infarction for the sudden onset, inflammation such as transverse myelitis or a compressing abscess for the one that evolved over days
That the sudden case needs no imaging
quiz.explanation: The examination places both lesions in the cord, and the time course chooses the cause. Onset over minutes points to an injury or a vascular event, and onset over days to inflammation, infection or a compressing collection. Identical examinations say nothing about a functional disorder, and a sensory level with retention is a structural pattern. Both children need urgent imaging.

quiz.question: A 2-year-old's parents report she has preferred her right hand since 7 months. She has no other complaints and has never lost skills. What is the most likely tempo, and what does it imply?
options: Regressive, so a neurodegenerative disease is likely
Normal, because handedness is established by 7 months
Episodic, so an EEG is the key test
Static, because hand preference before 12 months points to weakness of the left hand from an early lesion such as a perinatal stroke
quiz.explanation: Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand. A deficit present since infancy, with no lost skills, is static and fits an early fixed lesion such as a perinatal arterial stroke. Nothing has been lost, so this is not regression. Handedness develops after 12 months, and with no attacks the episodic tempo does not apply.

quiz.question: Why do validated positive signs of functional weakness make a strong case when present but a weak case when absent?
options: Because they have high specificity but low sensitivity
Because they have high sensitivity but low specificity
Because they are only valid in adults
Because they have never been studied
quiz.explanation: The validated positive signs have a specificity of 92 to 100%, but their sensitivity ranges from 8 to 100% and is often low (Daum 2014). A present sign is rarely found in structural disease, so it is strong evidence. Many patients with functional disorder lack any particular sign, so its absence proves little. The evidence is class III, and the principle applies in children too.

quiz.question: A short differential for an acute cord syndrome lists transverse myelitis first and epidural abscess fourth, by likelihood. What should determine which is investigated first?
options: Likelihood alone, so investigate transverse myelitis first
Cost alone, so do the cheapest test first
Both likelihood and the cost of missing it, and since a compressing abscess is treatable by urgent decompression, it must be excluded at once
The family's preference
quiz.explanation: Rank a short list by likelihood and by the cost of missing each diagnosis. A compressing epidural abscess is a surgical emergency in which delay costs function, so urgent spinal imaging comes first even if myelitis is more likely, and the same MRI usually answers both questions. Likelihood alone risks missing the emergency, and the price of the test is beside the point.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old born at 27 weeks has spastic diplegia: stiff legs, good hands, normal speech, and steady if slow progress in every skill. A gene panel sent by another team reports a variant of uncertain significance in a gene linked to a progressive white-matter disease. Her parents ask whether this changes her diagnosis. What is the best response?
options: Yes, because the variant lies in a relevant gene and the progressive disease should replace cerebral palsy as the diagnosis
Send a broader panel, because one uncertain result means the first panel was too narrow
Repeat brain imaging every six months until the variant is explained

Weigh the variant against a low prior, since the static course and the history of prematurity already fit and uncertain significance is not a diagnosis, and reopen the question if she ever begins to lose skills
quiz.explanation: Uncertain significance is the middle tier of the five-tier scale, neither pathogenic nor benign (Richards 2015), and its weight depends on the prior. This child's course is static, and spastic diplegia with good hands and speech after birth at 27 weeks already has an explanation (DeMyer, p. 340). A broader panel or serial imaging chases the variant. Regression would be the reason to look again.

signOff: The resident presents three new consults to a faculty reader in where, when, what form, stating the localization, the tempo and a ranked differential before any test results are known.

opener.parable: A test result behaves more like a witness than a judge. How much weight its evidence deserves depends on what you already knew when you called it, so the same report can mean a great deal in one child and very little in another.
opener.history: Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century English Presbyterian minister and amateur mathematician, gave his name to a rule clinicians use every day without naming it. The odds before a test, multiplied by the weight of its result, give the odds after.
